UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                               BEFORE THE
                 FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


Joint Application for Authorization under Section 203
                                                          Docket No. EC26-131-000
of the Federal Power Act of NextEra Energy, Inc. et al.




            MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF THE
              VIRGINIA OFFICE OF THE ATTORNEY GENERAL,
                    DIVISION OF CONSUMER COUNSEL




                                      October 30, 2026
                                UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                      BEFORE THE
                        FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


    Joint Application for Authorization under Section 203
                                                                            Docket No. EC26-131-000
    of the Federal Power Act of NextEra Energy, Inc. et al.




                  MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF THE
                    VIRGINIA OFFICE OF THE ATTORNEY GENERAL,
                          DIVISION OF CONSUMER COUNSEL



           Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC”

or the “Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1 the Virginia Office of the Attorney

General, Division of Consumer Counsel (“Virginia Consumer Counsel”) respectfully files this

Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer to the October 15, 2026 Motion for Leave to Answer

and Answer filed by NextEra Energy, Inc. (“NextEra”) and Dominion Energy, Inc. (“Dominion”)

(collectively, “Applicants”).2

           Applicants’ Answer glosses over the extraordinary nature of this proposed merger and the

risks to ratepayers inherent in its approach to large-load growth. Applicants seem to brush off calls

for a thorough evaluation of market power as being outside the scope of FERC’s review. The

Applicants are incorrect. The contexts of unprecedented demand, large load growth, evolving

market rules, and changes in the generation fleet are essential facts that FERC must consider in

Response”). FERC has separately noticed the Deficiency Response, and Virginia Consumer Counsel reserves all rights

 assessing the Application. The robust analysis requested by Virginia Consumer Counsel and

others3 is well within FERC’s authority.

                                 MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

           Rule 213(a)(2) generally does not allow answers to be made to answers. However, the

Commission has accepted such answers where they provide information that assists the

Commission in its decision-making process.4 Here, Virginia Consumer Counsel seeks to provide

information that will support FERC’s understanding of the issues presented and respectfully

requests that the Commission grant Virginia Consumer Counsel’s Motion for Leave to Answer

insofar as the Commission accepts the Applicants’ Answer.

                                                  ANSWER

           Applicants ask the Commission to review their proposed merger with blinders on. To do

so would be detrimental to the work that the Commission, PJM, and PJM’s stakeholders are doing

to protect affordability and reliability while supporting the remarkable load growth that is

underway. In order to approve this proposed merger, the Commission needs the ability to analyze

its potential impacts in light of attendant market reforms to remediate conditions the Commission

has found not to be just and reasonable, and the Commission must impose any and all conditions

necessary to protect the public interest. Accordingly, the Commission should require additional

criteria to inform the analysis of the proposed merger. Applicants themselves cite the governing




3
 See Protest of the Independent Market Monitor for PJM in Docket No. EC26-131 (Sept. 29, 2026), eLibrary No.
20260929-5147 (“PJM IMM Protest”); Protest and Request for Hearing of Attorneys General, State Energy and
Environmental Agencies, and State Ratepayer Advocates in Docket No. EC26-131 (Sept. 29, 2026), eLibrary No.
20260929-5077; Protest of Public Interest Organizations in Docket No. EC26-131 (Sept. 29, 2026), eLibrary No.
20260929-5165 (“PIOs Protest”).
4
    See, e.g., Grays Harbor Energy LLC, 196 FERC ¶ 61,186 (2026).

                                                        2
 standard: merger analysis should be “as forward-looking as practicable”. 5 Virginia Consumer

Counsel and other intervenors in this docket have identified omissions from and inconsistencies in

the Applicants’ analysis. Any assumptions made by the Applicants about resources and load

growth should be thoroughly examined, and they should be incorporated only if they are supported

and consistent. Regardless of ongoing market mitigation reform efforts, this is the Commission’s

responsibility.

     I.     The narrow review that Applicants request is antithetical to the Commission’s
            ongoing efforts to ensure just and reasonable rates in PJM.
       The Commission should not evaluate the proposed merger through a static, backward-looking

framework that disregards the profound structural changes now unfolding in PJM. Applicants urge

the Commission not to tailor its review to “the ‘size’ or ‘complexity’ of the combined company.”6

But as FERC recently explained: “The electric industry is in the midst of changes not seen in a

generation. Compared to more traditional load growth, the large loads seeking to connect to the

grid today are larger, sometimes by orders of magnitude, and more concentrated. . . . [T]hese

dynamics . . . create new challenges that, if unaddressed, could jeopardize the reliability and

affordability of the grid on which we all depend.”7

           Through its recent orders, the Commission has articulated concerns about the impacts of

load growth on just and reasonable rates for service.8 In its June 18, 2026 large load show cause

orders, the Commission found that “electricity demand in the United States is expected to grow at




5
    Applicants’ Answer at 22 n.79.
6
    Applicants’ Answer at 41.
7
 PJM Interconnection, et al., 195 FERC ¶ 61,211 (2026) (“June Show Cause Order”) (Rosner, Comm’r, concurring
at PP 3,5).
8
 Comments of the Virginia Office of the Attorney General, Division of Consumer Counsel, Docket No. EC26-131
(Sept. 29, 2026), eLibrary No. 20260929-5155 (“Virginia Consumer Counsel Comments”).

                                                     3
 an extraordinary pace in the near term, largely due to the rapid growth of large loads.” 9 The

Commission described the challenge as urgent: “The records in these proceedings illustrate a host

of urgent challenges associated with providing the transmission service needed to serve the

ongoing influx of large loads while maintaining reliability and affordability.”10 The Commission

also emphasized the need to prevent cost shifting from large loads to residential and small business

customers.11 As these statements demonstrate, large load growth is a structural challenge with

direct implications for consumer protection and cost responsibility. In June, Chairman Swett

highlighted the “monumental, generational and ‘urgent’ challenge FERC must solve for our

country” and the need for “‘reforms to ensure the timely and orderly interconnection of large loads

to the transmission system.’”12 Those reforms will be impaired by a merger designed to capitalize

on uncertainty surrounding the very issues that FERC seeks to address in its show cause orders.

            Yet, the Applicants’ Answer insists that the Commission must confine its review to current

market conditions and rely exclusively on the Delivered Price Test,13 an analysis with recognized

limitations.14 This position is incompatible with the Commission’s responsibility under the Federal

Power Act and is inconsistent with the Commission’s stated policy goal of protecting consumers

from the risk of rapid large load growth.

            Section 203 requires the Commission to determine whether a transaction is consistent with

the public interest, a standard that necessarily encompasses foreseeable future conditions when


9
    June Show Cause Order, P 6.
10
     Id. P 1.
11
  Id. P 77 (“We next preliminarily find that PJM’s Tariff appears to be unjust and unreasonable because it lacks
adequate mechanisms to mitigate the risk of cost shifting among transmission customers, which may result in unjust
and unreasonable rates for transmission service.”)
12

13

 those conditions are not speculative but instead are certain, measurable, and already reshaping the

market.15 PJM is experiencing extraordinary load growth driven by data centers, electrification,

and industrial development. Load growth in PJM has already produced reliability warnings,

capacity shortfalls, and transmission constraints. 16 These developments do not present merely

speculative or hypothetical risks; they are current realities with reasonably certain downstream

consequences that a public-interest analysis of this transaction should confront.

            The PJM Independent Market Monitor (“IMM”) has made this point unmistakably clear in

this proceeding: PJM is facing unprecedented load growth that materially alters competitive

dynamics and increases the risk that large suppliers will be able to exercise market power in ways

the Delivered Price Test is not designed to detect. 17 As the IMM explained: “The impact on

competition from the growth of load from data centers is the most critical issue affecting PJM

markets and the public interest in competitive outcomes today.” 18 The IMM warned that the

traditional Section 203 screens rely “on a view of markets from before competitive wholesale

power markets existed, fail[] to consider the actual current and evolving competitive environment,

and fail[] to look forward and recognize the effects on the incentives for the entry of new,

innovative, competitive suppliers of generation and transmission in PJM and other markets.”19 The

IMM further emphasized that the Delivered Price Test does not account for the impact on

competition from two major transmission owners in PJM. “With generation and energy markets

already experiencing consolidation, the proposed combination of the two major transmission

 owners raises concerns of both horizontal and vertical market power.”20 These concerns are not

abstract. They reflect PJM’s own operational experience and its public statements regarding the

challenges posed by accelerating demand. The IMM’s explanation of current market conditions

demonstrates why the proposed merger must be evaluated using forward-looking parameters:

because they define the market in which the merged entity would operate.

            These forward-looking concerns are the current industry reality and are not only recognized

by the IMM and the Commission; they are expressly acknowledged by NextEra itself. In public

statements describing the strategic rationale for the merger, NextEra has repeatedly emphasized

that the transaction is designed to position the combined company to capture investment

opportunities created by large load growth. The Applicants have stated that they “expect the

combined company will deliver a compelling long-term shareholder value…” as a “[b]est in class

shareholder value proposition…” because of “[u]nmatched large load opportunity”. 21 The

Applicants have also stated that: “Since 2021, NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy have built

more generation than the next 25 largest utilities combined,”22 a merged entity market position

which should be of concern to the Commission. They have also stated that the “combined company

would have unmatched scale, capabilities and opportunities” including a “[c]ombined large-load

customer pipeline of 130+ GW.”23 Despite these statements of intention, the market power study

 provided by the Applicants includes only 830 MW of capacity within the entire PJM footprint.24

This limited analysis cannot reasonably be used to support a public interest finding.

           Further, these statements confirm that the Applicants themselves view large load growth

not as a speculative possibility but as a central, foreseeable, and monetizable feature of PJM’s

future market conditions. They also demonstrate that the merger is expressly intended to position

the Applicants to benefit from the very scarcity conditions, transmission constraints, and

infrastructure needs that the IMM and the Commission have identified as issues that have created

critical consumer protection concerns. Relying on a static analysis that ignores these foreseeable

conditions and constraints would fail to protect consumers and would not satisfy the Commission’s

statutory obligations.

     II.    The Commission should require supplemental analysis using additional criteria.
           Applicants say Virginia Consumer Counsel seeks to inject speculative data into the

analysis. 25 To the contrary, Virginia Consumer Counsel has asked the Commission to apply

objective criteria, applied market-wide and disclosed project-by-project, in order to effectively

evaluate contract expirations, retirements, generation additions, transmission upgrades, and load

commitments relevant to this merger.

           Specifically, the Commission should require supplemental study years or sensitivities

through 2028–2030. Each study should compare competitive conditions with and without the

transaction using the same supported assumptions concerning load, transmission availability,

retirements, and third-party entry. The material difference should be whether Applicants’ resources

appears to be updated from the July application. See Joint Application for Authorization Under Section 203 of the

20260715-5205 (listing 799 MW in the PJM footprint).

 and contractual interests remain independently controlled or are combined. This comparison would

distinguish transaction-related effects from changes that would occur regardless of the merger.

           Known contract expirations should also be distinguished from contingent renewals.

Retirements, generation with executed interconnection agreements, and approved transmission

upgrades should be evaluated according to their supporting milestones and anticipated timing.

Load under service agreements and construction authorizations should be examined for their

contractual conditions and expected demand before determining their treatment in the base case.

Earlier-stage developments may be assessed with appropriate sensitivities.

           Additionally, investor forecasts and business-planning assumptions should be reconciled

with the competitive analysis rather than automatically treated as proof that every identified

opportunity will occur. Applicants treat the same future developments differently depending on

the audience. To investors, Dominion reports more than 53 GW of data center capacity in various

stages of contracting.26 Before the Commission, however, Applicants characterize developments

beyond the 2027 study year as “highly speculative.”27 Applicants should reconcile these positions

and should explain material differences and identify evidence supporting their selected

assumptions.28

  For example, Applicants identify September 30, 2029, and December 31, 2029, expiration dates for the relevant
Millstone and Seabrook agreements, respectively. Applicants’ Answer at 13 n.50. Their current attribution of
contracted capacity to the purchasers rests on the existing commitments. Id. at 13-14. Applicants’ expectation of
recontracting does not establish the counterparty, quantity, duration, or allocation of control under a replacement
agreement. Id. At 19. Existing expiration dates and contingent replacement transactions should therefore be treated as
separate assumptions. Where material, Applicants should test supported alternatives while incorporating other relevant
market developments consistently.

            And further, for each material project or contract, Applicants should identify whether it is

included, excluded, or addressed through a sensitivity; explain that treatment; and identify the

affected market and study period. Such documentation would implement the requirement that the

screen’s data, assumptions, techniques, and conclusions are supported. 29 Virginia Consumer

Counsel requests this analysis because it is necessary to determine whether mitigation is warranted,

without prejudging that determination.

 III.       The Commission’s standard requires a forward-looking analysis
           The Applicants’ assertion that the Commission is legally prohibited from considering

future market conditions is incorrect. Nothing in Section 203 limits the Commission to present-

day market snapshots. Applicants argue that consideration of developments beyond their selected

study period would introduce speculative assumptions. 30 But the governing standard is clear:

merger analysis should be “as forward-looking as practicable.”31 The standard necessarily calls for

examination of the evidence supporting particular developments rather than the Applicants’

categorical exclusions based on an arbitrary time frame. The one-year cutoff that Applicants

propose32 is hardly as forward-looking as practicable.

           The Applicants’ position is not demanded by case law as they suggest. For example, in

Atlas, the Commission considered planned retirements approximately two and four years into the

future when evaluating whether the merged entity would become pivotal in the COMED capacity

market. 33 The Commission identified concrete support for considering those retirements: the

Although that decision does not require inclusion of every possible proposed project, it

demonstrates that later developments warrant consideration when supported by identifiable

milestones. Applicants should explain why comparable evidence does or does not support

examining particular developments beyond their self-selected study period.

           Applicants rely on Great Plains to support their proposal for a static analysis, but that case

does not establish a categorical prohibition against any later-period analysis. 35 There, the

Commission found the proposed future analysis speculative because other generation and

transmission developments would also change market conditions, and those changing

circumstances were kept constant in the assumptions. The Commission also emphasized that the

applicants had incorporated known and measurable changes into their selected test year. 36 In this

proceeding, Virginia Consumer Counsel seeks consistent treatment across the relevant markets,

rather than the addition of selected projects while all other assumptions remain fixed.

           Applicants’ own treatment of future developments demonstrates that they consider

developments beyond their selected screening period to be relevant as well. For example,

Applicants state that recontracting of Millstone and Seabrook after 2029 is “possible if not

likely.” 37 They also offer to accept certain resource-deactivation protections for capacity

commitment periods extending through June 2033 if the Commission determines those protections

are necessary. 38 This conditional offer does not establish a required screening horizon, but it

 confirms that certain identifiable developments beyond the selected study period are relevant to

 IV.         The Commission should closely examine Applicants’ projected load growth.
            To review the proposed merger, the Commission should parse Applicants’ large load

pipeline and make determinations on what is most reasonable to include in their analysis. In

announcing the merger, Applicants identified a combined large load pipeline of more than 130

GW, of which approximately 51 GW was associated with Dominion Energy Virginia.39 Dominion

has since reported that its Virginia data center pipeline grew to more than 53 GW as of mid-2026:

approximately 12 GW under executed Electric Service Agreements (“ESAs”), 9 GW under

Construction Letters of Authorization (“CLOAs”), and 32 GW under Substation Engineering

Letters of Authorization (“SELOAs”).40 These categories reflect different stages of development

and do not establish that the entire pipeline constitutes committed demand. More advanced

commitments, such as ESAs and CLOAs, should be evaluated according to their contractual

conditions and anticipated timing. Applicants should at least identify the conditions, expected

timing, and anticipated demand associated with each category, and reconcile those figures with the

load already incorporated into their forecasts. Applicants should also explain any material

differences between the assumptions in their public descriptions of expected growth and those

used in their competitive analysis.

            NextEra’s relatively small modeled presence in PJM and the Dominion zone explains why

the screen shows so little overlap with Dominion’s generation and such small HHI changes.41 But

that modeled presence only reflects generation brought online before June 1, 2027. It does not

 represent how NextEra’s planned entry in PJM, which Applicants exclude as outside the study

year, should be evaluated based on the supporting evidence.

            Applicants’ timing claim does not justify excluding NextEra’s queued projects. To support

excluding anticipated capacity resources from the analysis, Applicants assert that none of

NextEra’s generation currently in the PJM queue is expected to receive an interconnection

agreement before the first half of 2028.42 This assertion does not indicate when agreements are

expected to be executed or when the projects are expected to enter service. It also does not explain

why each anticipated material project should be excluded from every later-period sensitivity.

            Applicants should disclose project-level queue status, study progress, anticipated

agreement and commercial-operation dates, and necessary upgrades, and explain remaining

contingencies. This means the Applicants should include, for instance, the approximately 4.3 GW

of development in southwestern Pennsylvania discussed in the Answer. 43 The competitive

significance of this anticipated project should be evaluated using location and deliverability into

the relevant markets. Granted that not every planned NextEra project would affect the competitive

market analysis, and a project’s presence in PJM alone does not establish that it would compete in

every constrained submarket; the relevant question is whether a project’s location and

deliverability would allow for competition with Dominion’s generation in those markets.

            Other intervenors raise related concerns. The IMM argues that Applicants’ analysis does

not account for planned generation and transmission and identifies a potential relationship between

NextEra’s Pennsylvania development and constraints affecting the Dominion Zone and

Chesapeake submarket.44 The Public Interest Organizations contend that the Delivered Price Test

 does not adequately capture emerging bilateral capacity arrangements associated with large

loads. 45 To address those concerns and the concerns of Virginia Consumer Counsel, the

Commission should examine the underlying assumptions and transaction-specific effects.

     V.     Applicants’ response concerning broader PJM issues does not resolve the
            transaction-specific questions
           Applicants contend that general concerns about PJM’s structure and mitigation rules

belong in other proceedings.46 Virginia Consumer Counsel’s request concerns the combination of

Applicants’ existing holdings, contractual interests, and supported future development under

common ownership. The Commission can examine that combination without resolving every

disputed aspect of PJM’s market design, and it must do so in order to approve the merger.

           The relevant question is whether the transaction changes independent supply alternatives

under supported future conditions, particularly in constrained markets. Additional analysis is

necessary to complete and review the supplemental comparisons, material project and contract

disclosures, and reconciliation of import allocations requested here. Broader market reform efforts

will support and parallel this analysis, but the pendency of those efforts should not substitute for

the forward-looking analysis imperative to assessing this proposed merger.

                                            CONCLUSION

           For these reasons, Virginia Consumer Counsel urges the Commission to reject the

Applicants’ argument that Section 203 prohibits forward-looking analysis. The Commission

should instead acknowledge that PJM’s structural challenges demand a comprehensive review that

accounts for future load growth and its implications for competition, reliability, and consumer

protection. These challenges are documented by the PJM Independent Market Monitor, recognized


45
     PIOs Protests at 23–24.
46
     Applicants’ Answer at 31–32.

                                                  13
 in the Commission’s own large load show cause orders, and openly described by NextEra as the

investment thesis for the proposed merger. A merger between entities of this scale in a region

experiencing unprecedented demand pressures cannot be evaluated solely through a static,

backward-looking framework that assumes tomorrow will resemble today, particularly where the

Applicants’ own supporting materials contradict this assumption. In light of the extraordinary

developments in the PJM market and this extraordinary proposal to merge two large and dynamic

utilities, the public interest standard necessitates a forward-looking analysis framework, and the

Commission should exercise its statutory authority accordingly.




                                     Respectfully submitted,
